opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think it's a good question, and the honest answer is that it's mixed. It depends a lot on what kind of concern you mean.

If the concern is something concrete and near-term, like a deployed model doing something it shouldn't, or someone on the team noticing a new kind of misuse, I think we can actually move pretty fast. There are established processes. People know who to talk to, and there's a fairly short path from "someone noticed a problem" to "someone with authority is looking at it." In those cases the organization's size is often an asset, because there are lots of people with relevant expertise and the infrastructure to act.

Where it gets harder is with more speculative or conceptual concerns. Say someone on the safety team comes up with a new argument for why some training approach might produce models with subtly misaligned goals. That doesn't come with an obvious incident attached, so you can't point to the thing going wrong. You're asking people to change plans based on reasoning about something that hasn't happened yet. That's just a harder sell in any large organization, and Google DeepMind is a large organization. There are many stakeholders, many teams with their own priorities and timelines, and changing course means convincing a lot of people.

So a lot of what we try to do on the AGI safety side is lay the groundwork ahead of time. We try to build relationships with the teams that actually train and ship models, so that when we raise something, it isn't coming from an unfamiliar group nobody has worked with. We also try to get frameworks agreed in advance, things like the Frontier Safety Framework, where you specify conditions and corresponding responses before you're in the moment. Then if a model hits some capability threshold, you aren't arguing from scratch about whether to do anything. You've already agreed that crossing this line triggers these mitigations. That makes responding quickly much more feasible, because the hard deliberation happened earlier.

I'd also say I don't think "fast" should be the only goal. Sometimes a concern turns out to be less serious than it first looked, and an organization that pivots hard on every new worry won't get much done and will lose credibility internally. What you really want is to respond quickly to the things that matter while having a good filter for what matters. I think we're reasonably good at that. I wouldn't claim we're perfect, and I'd like us to be better at taking the more speculative risks seriously before there's a concrete demonstration. A lot of my effort goes into trying to make that happen.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the honest answer is that it's a mixed picture, and it depends a lot on what kind of safety concern you're talking about.

On the fast end, if a concern is something like "this model is producing a particular kind of harmful output" or "we've found a jailbreak that lets people get around a mitigation," that's the kind of thing where the response can actually be pretty quick. There are teams whose job it is to watch for that stuff, there are escalation paths, and the fixes are often things you can do at the level of fine-tuning or filters or system prompts. So you're talking days to weeks, not months. And I'd say that's genuinely improved over the last few years, partly because there's just been more practice at it.

The slower end is when the concern is about something more fundamental. If you come in and say, "I think the way we're doing reinforcement learning is systematically producing models with goals we don't understand," that's not something you fix with a patch. It requires people to agree that it's actually a problem, it requires research to figure out what the alternative even is, and it requires buy-in from the parts of the organization that are building the models and are under a lot of pressure to ship. And at that scale, a large organization is just not going to turn on a dime. There are a lot of stakeholders, there are a lot of commitments already made, and there's a reasonable prior that most new alarming-sounding concerns don't pan out, so the bar for "this should change how we do things" is appropriately high.

Something I'd add is that we've tried to build structures that make the slower case faster than it would otherwise be. The Frontier Safety Framework is the clearest example, where the idea is you commit in advance to what you'd do if a model hit certain capability thresholds, so that when it happens you're not debating from scratch under time pressure. You've already had the argument. Whether that works as intended is something we'll really only find out when it gets stress-tested, and I try to be honest that it's not a guarantee.

And then the thing I'd flag as the real bottleneck is often not organizational will, it's technical. Even when everyone agrees a concern is serious, if we don't have good enough tools to detect the problem or measure whether a fix worked, we can't respond quickly no matter how motivated we are. That's a lot of why I think interpretability and evaluations matter so much. They're what convert "we're worried" into "we can actually act on this in a reasonable timeframe."

So overall I'd say: reasonably good at the tactical stuff, slower and more uncertain on the deep stuff, and the thing that would most improve response time is better science, not just better process.

astra-6.text:
I think it depends a lot on what kind of safety concern we’re talking about. If you have a concrete demonstration of a problem, a clear explanation of why it matters, and something you can do about it, that’s much easier for an organization to respond to quickly. If the concern is more speculative, or people disagree about what would count as addressing it, then things tend to take longer.

My sense is that Google DeepMind has both the technical expertise and people who are motivated to take these concerns seriously. But that’s different from saying that the whole organization can turn on a dime. You need the concern to reach the right people, you need someone to own the response, and you need a way to tell whether the response actually helped.

So I’m cautiously optimistic, but I wouldn’t want our safety strategy to depend entirely on reacting quickly. A lot of the work is setting things up beforehand so that, when a concern comes up, we already know how to investigate it and how it should affect decisions.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it depends a lot on what kind of concern we’re talking about. If you identify a concrete problem and there’s a reasonably clear intervention, I think Google DeepMind can move quite quickly. There are people who care a lot about safety and want to fix things when they see something going wrong.

The harder case is when the concern is more speculative, or people disagree about how serious it is, or addressing it would require a substantial change in what the organisation is doing. Then you need to build a shared understanding of the problem and get the relevant people on board. That can take time.

So I’d distinguish having the capacity to respond quickly from reliably recognising when a quick response is needed. I’m more optimistic about the former. The latter is a difficult problem, and it’s part of why you want to do the thinking and establish processes ahead of time.
